Game: Four dots sit on one circle and three sloping lines leave the point P. Watch the three places where they cross the sides of the triangle.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or P with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Move the angle slider, tick the boxes to see the matching triangles and circles, and press Next pair.
90
Look for the math

Move P anywhere on the circle and tilt the three lines as you like: the three crossing points still fall on one straight line. That is the little theorem behind this drawing.

Three feet, one line

Let A', B' and C' be the points where the lines from P meet the sides BC, CA and AB. Every line leaves P at the same angle to its side. The theorem due to Lazare Carnot says those three feet are collinear whenever P lies on the triangle's circumcircle. The logic test measures the signed area of triangle A'B'C' on more than a thousand drawings, at every slider angle, and it is zero each time. Push P off the circle and the line breaks — the circle is really needed.

Why they line up

The angle at P between two of the lines equals the angle at the matching vertex of the triangle, so P, two feet and two vertices form cyclic quadrilaterals. Equal angles in those circles give equal angles at the feet, and then similar triangles give three length ratios. Multiplied together they cancel:

AC'/C'B × BA'/A'C × CB'/B'A = 1

in ordinary lengths, or −1 with directed lengths. That is exactly the Menelaus theorem, so the feet must lie on a line. Tick the two boxes and press Next pair to see the circles and shaded triangles that carry the equal angles.

Turning the lines

At 90° the three lines are perpendicular to the sides and the line through the feet is the Simson line (also called Wallace's line). The applet's slider goes from 5° to 160° (its Java scrollbar has maximum 170 with a visible amount of 10): the feet still line up because "equally inclined" does not have to mean "at right angles". The original applet keeps A, B, C and P on its starting circle, and this page does the same.

A different Carnot theorem

Another cut-the-knot article, Carnot's Theorem, states a different result about perpendiculars meeting at one point: AC'² − BC'² + BA'² − CA'² + CB'² − AB'² = 0. The logic test confirms that identity at 90°, where the three lines here do meet at P, and confirms that it fails at other angles. This page follows the applet's own page, which is about the line through the feet, not that squared-length sum.

Set the slider to 90°, drag P round the circle and watch the green line swing. Then try 5° and press Next pair to find the equal angles in the circles.
